A researcher follows two groups of people to assess for the development of dementia. One group has a history of lorazepam use and the other does not. What type of study design is being used?
explanation_text:
Study Designs — Prospective vs Retrospective Cohort Correct: C. Prospective cohort — you group people by EXPOSURE (lorazepam use vs none) and follow them FORWARD in time to see who develops the outcome (dementia).
Retrospective cohort (D): same exposure→outcome logic, but the outcome already happened and you reconstruct it from old records.
Case-control (B): starts from the OUTCOME (dementia vs not) and looks BACKWARD for exposures — opposite direction.
Case series (A): describes patients with no comparison group. RCT (E): investigator assigns the exposure; here patients chose it, so not randomized.
Hook: Cohort = pick by exposure, follow forward. Case-control = pick by disease, look back.

stem: Disruption in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit function is most closely associated with what group of disorders?
explanation_text:
CSTC Circuit & OCD Correct: E. Obsessive-compulsive disorder. The cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical (CSTC) loop runs orbitofrontal cortex + anterior cingulate → striatum (caudate) → thalamus → back to cortex. An overactive loop keeps a “something is wrong” signal running — the brain basis of obsessions and the urge to perform compulsions.
Why it fits: SSRIs and CBT (and DBS/cingulotomy in severe cases) calm this loop; imaging shows OFC/caudate/cingulate hyperactivity that normalizes with treatment.
Distractors: Mood, schizophrenia, somatoform, and PTSD map onto other networks (monoamine/limbic, mesolimbic dopamine, fear circuitry), not the classic CSTC overactivity.
Hook: CSTC = the “worry loop” stuck in the ON position.

stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department after a syncopal episode with hyperthermia, headache, flushing, and tachycardia. The patient has significant hypotension requiring fluid resuscitation. According to the family, the patient has a history of schizophrenia, generalized anxiety disorder, and alcohol use disorder. An Interaction with which of the following medications is most likely to have caused the patient's symptoms?
explanation_text:
Disulfiram–Alcohol Reaction Correct: B. Disulfiram. It blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so any alcohol makes acetaldehyde pile up fast → flushing, throbbing headache, nausea/vomiting, sweating, tachycardia, and hypotension. The deliberately miserable reaction is what discourages drinking.
Clinical clue: alcohol use disorder + sudden flushing, hyperthermia, and hypotension after a drink = disulfiram (acetaldehyde) reaction.
Distractors: amitriptyline (anticholinergic/overdose), fluoxetine (serotonin), haloperidol (EPS/NMS), and lorazepam (sedation) do not cause an acetaldehyde flush with alcohol.
Hook: Disulfiram = a “hangover on command.”

answer_raw: A. Attachment between a parent and child
explanation_text:
Ainsworth’s Strange Situation: Attachment Correct: A. Attachment between parent and child. A 12–18-month-old is watched through separations from and reunions with the caregiver; how the infant uses the parent as a “secure base” and reacts at reunion defines the attachment style.
Patterns: Secure (distressed at separation, soothed at reunion); Insecure-avoidant (indifferent); Insecure-ambivalent/resistant (clingy yet hard to console); Disorganized (confused/fearful, linked to maltreatment).
Distractors: B is Piaget (cognition); C and D describe shared mentalizing and affect regulation; E is internal working models — none is what this paradigm measures.
Hook: Strange Situation = a test of how a baby uses the parent as “home base.”

stem: A 72-year-old patient presents with subacute onset of progressive ataxia of gait and limbs. Laboratory testing reveals the presence of an anti-Yo antibody in the serum. Which of the following tests should be ordered next?

options.text: Single-photon emission computed tomography scan of the brain
Computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain

answer_text: Computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
answer_raw: B. Computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
explanation_text:
Anti-Yo: Paraneoplastic Cerebellar Degeneration Correct: B. CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Subacute cerebellar ataxia + anti-Yo (anti-PCA-1) antibody = paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration. The antibody is a red flag for a hidden cancer — anti-Yo is classically tied to ovarian and breast cancer — so the next step is to FIND the tumor.
Why not the others: brain MRI/SPECT are usually normal or nonspecific in this antibody-mediated process; serial anti-Yo titers don’t change management; spine MRI targets the wrong region.
Key idea: a paraneoplastic antibody means “hunt for the tumor,” because treating the cancer is the best chance to halt the neurologic decline.
Hook: Anti-Yo → look at the Ovaries (and breast).

stem: A nine-year-old child with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder does not respond to methylphenidate. Which of the following medications should be tried next?
explanation_text:
ADHD: Switching Stimulant Classes Correct: E. Dextroamphetamine. If a child fails one stimulant CLASS (methylphenidate), the best next step is to try the OTHER class — an amphetamine — before switching to a non-stimulant. Many kids who don’t respond to one class respond well to the other, and stimulants remain first-line because they’re the most effective ADHD treatment.
Distractors: clonidine and guanfacine (alpha-2 agonists), atomoxetine, and bupropion/fluoxetine are second-line — reserved for when both stimulant classes fail or aren’t tolerated.
Hook: methylphenidate flop → try an amphetamine before going non-stimulant.

Over the course of several months, a 46-year-old patient with no past psychiatric history becomes emotionally labile and Irritable. The patient undergoes personality changes, and is observed to Inappropriately laugh when neighborhood children taunt a stray cat. Within two years, the patient develops a fear of contamination and greatly decreases food intake due to being convinced that all food has germs. Memory is preserved. The patient is no longer able to work or live independently. Neuropsychiatric tests show impaired language and attention. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) Correct: C. Frontotemporal dementia. Giveaways: early personality/behavior change and disinhibition (loss of empathy — laughing at a tormented cat), then compulsive/odd behaviors and language decline, all with MEMORY relatively PRESERVED, in a younger patient (40s–60s). FTD strikes the frontal and temporal lobes first (often tau or TDP-43 pathology).
Why not the others: Alzheimer leads with MEMORY loss; Lewy body brings visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, and fluctuations; schizophrenia rarely starts at 46 with steady decline; OCD doesn’t cause progressive aphasia and functional collapse.
Hook: behavior/personality change first + memory spared = frontotemporal, not Alzheimer.

stem: Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for postpartum depression?
explanation_text:
Postpartum Depression: Strongest Risk Factor Correct: E. Untreated depression during pregnancy. The strongest predictor of postpartum depression is depression or anxiety already present and untreated DURING pregnancy — it simply continues past delivery. That’s why we screen and treat mood symptoms antenatally, not just after birth.
Other (weaker) risks: personal/family history of depression, poor social support, marital conflict, stressful life events, low SES. Reproductive hormone LEVELS don’t correlate well — it’s sensitivity to hormonal shifts that matters.
Hook: the best predictor of depression after birth is depression before birth.

In cases of severe lithium toxicity, extracorporeal treatment is typically indicated. Lithium is readily dialyzable due to its:
explanation_text:
Why Lithium Is Dialyzable Correct: C. Low molecular weight. Lithium is a tiny, sodium-like ion that is NOT protein-bound and sits in the body water, so it slips across the dialysis membrane easily — making hemodialysis the treatment for severe lithium toxicity.
Why not the others: high protein binding or high tissue binding would TRAP a drug; a high volume of distribution also limits removal. Low molecular weight + minimal protein binding = readily dialyzed.
Clinical note: watch for rebound rises as lithium redistributes out of tissues after dialysis.
Hook: small, water-soluble, and unbound → easy to pull out by dialysis.

stem: Which of the following is among the first medications ever approved to treat depression?
explanation_text:
History: The First Antidepressant Correct: B. Iproniazid. In the early 1950s it was developed as a TUBERCULOSIS drug — but clinicians noticed TB patients became unusually euphoric and energized. That accident revealed it was a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI); by the late 1950s it became one of the first drugs used for depression and helped launch the monoamine theory of mood.
Distractors: chlorpromazine was the first ANTIPSYCHOTIC; lithium treats mania; desipramine is a later TCA; methylphenidate is a stimulant.
Hook: the first antidepressant was a happy accident on a TB ward.

stem: A graduate student is brought to the emergency department during exam week because of the sudden onset of paralysis in the right leg. On physical exam, reflexes are normal. The doctor asks the patient to lie down flat and lift the unaffected leg. When the patient does this, the doctor feels increased pressure under the affected leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Functional Neurological Disorder & Hoover’s Sign Correct: B. Functional Neurological (Conversion) Disorder. The clue is HOOVER’S SIGN: when the patient lifts the healthy leg, the examiner feels the “paralyzed” leg involuntarily push DOWN — proving the motor pathway works. Symptoms are real and involuntary but incompatible with neurologic disease, often triggered by stress (exam week), with normal reflexes.
Why not the others: Factitious = consciously faked for the sick role; Illness anxiety = fear of disease without deficits; Somatic symptom disorder = excessive distress about real symptoms; hypokalemic periodic paralysis shows abnormal reflexes/labs.
Hook: Hoover’s sign positive = functional, not structural.

A celebrity radio psychiatrist tells the listening audience that medications like alprazolam are often prescribed for insomnia. A radio listener obtains alprazolam 1 mg tablets from a friend. The listener takes four tablets, falls, and sustains a sprained wrist and a concussion. The listener is now suing the psychiatrist for malpractice. Which of the following is the most likely outcome of this case?

options.text: Psychiatrist will win because the patient was not sufficiently injured.
Patient will win because the concussion can have long-term effects.
Patient will win because the psychiatrist deviated from the standard of care.
Patient will win because the higher dose he took directly mediated the injury.
Psychiatrist will win because a doctor-patient relationship was not established

answer_text: Psychiatrist will win because a doctor-patient relationship was not established
answer_raw: E. Psychiatrist will win because a doctor-patient relationship was not established
explanation_text:
Malpractice Needs a Doctor–Patient Relationship Correct: E. The psychiatrist wins because no doctor–patient relationship was established. Malpractice requires the 4 D’s: Duty, Dereliction (breach of that duty), Direct causation, and Damages. A Duty exists only once a doctor–patient relationship forms. General advice broadcast to a radio audience creates no individual relationship — so there is no duty, and the claim fails.
Why not the others: the listener was genuinely injured and took a high dose, but without a duty those facts don’t create liability; “deviation from standard of care” © only matters once a duty exists.
Hook: no relationship → no duty → no malpractice.

When observed in a young adult, bilateral paresis of the medial rectus muscle of the eye on attempted lateral gaze, with a coarse nystagmus in the abducting eye, is characteristic of which of the following conditions?
explanation_text:
Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) → MS Correct: A. Multiple sclerosis. Failure to ADDUCT one eye on lateral gaze plus coarse nystagmus in the ABDUCTING eye = internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO), from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) that disconnects CN VI from the contralateral CN III. BILATERAL INO in a YOUNG adult is classic for MS (MLF demyelination).
Why not the others: a small pontine infarct also causes INO but usually older and unilateral; PCP gives vertical/rotary nystagmus; Wernicke causes gaze palsy + ataxia + confusion; CN III palsy gives a “down-and-out” eye with ptosis, not isolated adduction failure.
Hook: young + bilateral INO = MS (an MLF problem).

stem: A patient describes hearing his name each time the wind rustles the leaves outside his room each morning. Which of the following describes this phenomenon?
explanation_text:
Illusion vs Hallucination Correct: A. Illusion. An illusion is a MISinterpretation of a REAL external stimulus — real rustling leaves are misperceived as his name. There IS a true sensory input; the brain just misreads it.
Contrast: a hallucination has NO external stimulus at all. Hypnagogic (falling asleep) and hypnopompic (waking) hallucinations happen at sleep–wake transitions and can be normal. Synesthesia = one sense triggers another (seeing colors when hearing music). Derealization = the world feels unreal or detached.
Hook: real stimulus misread = illusion; no stimulus = hallucination.

A patient in early remission from alcohol dependence presents to the psychiatrist reporting intense craving for alcohol. The patient is having difficulty managing the cravings and is concerned about relapsing. In addition to providing psychosocial interventions, which of the following medications would be most appropriate to recommend for this patient?
explanation_text:
Alcohol Craving: Naltrexone Correct: C. Naltrexone. An opioid-receptor antagonist that blunts the dopamine “reward” from drinking, so it cuts craving and heavy-drinking days — first-line for active craving and can be started while the patient is still drinking.
Why the others are wrong: B. Disulfiram doesn’t reduce craving — it only makes you ill if you drink (aversion) and needs a highly motivated, abstinent patient. A. Topiramate can lower craving but is off-label/second-line, not the best initial pick. D. Ondansetron is investigational (mainly early-onset subtypes), not standard. E. Lorazepam treats withdrawal, not craving, and risks cross-dependence in alcohol use disorder.
Hook: craving → naltrexone (kills the reward); disulfiram = punishment, not craving.

stem: A patient presents to the emergency department with significant paranoia. The patient is hypervigilant, pacing, and responding to unseen others. Which of the following techniques would be most appropriate to establish rapport with the patient?

options.text: Agree that the patient's suspiciousness is justified

Rapport with a Paranoid Patient Correct: B. Acknowledge the patient’s fear. With an acutely paranoid, hypervigilant, hallucinating patient, empathizing with the underlying FEAR (“this seems really frightening”) is non-threatening and builds trust without endorsing the delusion.
Why the others are wrong: A. Sustained eye contact can feel confrontational and threatening to a paranoid patient. C. Directly confronting the paranoia provokes defensiveness and wrecks rapport. D. Agreeing the suspicions are justified colludes with and reinforces the delusion. E. Acting like a “close friend” is falsely familiar, can heighten suspicion, and crosses a professional boundary.
Hook: validate the emotion (fear), not the delusion — stay calm and non-threatening.

stem: The psychiatrist evaluates an 18-year-old patient who has been avoiding food for the last four months. Her BMI is less than normal, and she menstruates regularly. Family members report that the patient obsesses about being "fat," even though she continues to lose weight. On several occasions, they have overheard her vomiting in the bathroom after consuming a large meal. The patient meets criteria for which of the following diagnoses?
explanation_text:
Anorexia (Binge-Purge) vs Bulimia Correct: B. Anorexia nervosa. The deciding feature is LOW body weight (BMI below normal) plus intense fear of fatness and distorted body image. She also purges, but because she is UNDERWEIGHT this is anorexia nervosa, binge-eating/purging type — not bulimia.
Why the others are wrong: A. Bulimia requires NORMAL or above-normal weight; if underweight, anorexia takes precedence. C. Rumination = effortless regurgitation, no weight/shape concern. D. Unspecified eating disorder is used only when full criteria aren’t met. E. ARFID = food avoidance WITHOUT any fear of weight gain or body-image disturbance.
Hook: purging + underweight = anorexia; purging + normal weight = bulimia.

stem: A 35-year-old patient is hospitalized because of a concussion after a motor vehicle collision. Physical examination shows no abnormalities other than minor lacerations and ecchymoses. One week later, the patient has generalized pain, dizziness, difficulty sleeping, and recurrent nightmares when able to sleep. The patient now fears driving. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the development of these symptoms?
explanation_text:
Acute Stress Disorder vs PTSD (Timing) Correct: C. Acute stress disorder. After a traumatic event (the MVC), intrusive nightmares, hyperarousal/insomnia, dissociation, and avoidance (fear of driving) lasting 3 days to 1 month = acute stress disorder. Here the symptoms are at ONE WEEK.
Why the others are wrong: E. PTSD has the SAME symptoms but is diagnosed only once they persist BEYOND 1 month — too early here. B. Adjustment disorder follows a stressor that need not be life-threatening and lacks the full trauma cluster. D. Somatic symptom disorder is excessive worry about physical symptoms, not trauma re-experiencing. A. Malingering = consciously faking for external gain, not suggested here.
Hook: same trauma symptoms — under 1 month = acute stress disorder; over 1 month = PTSD.

In a properly conducted randomized clinical trial, it is inappropriate to include p values in a table showing baseline characteristics of subjects by treatment group because:

options.text: standard errors should be reported instead.
p values cannot be calculated for categorical variables.
p values are often misleading without correction for multiple comparisons.
any differences at baseline must have arisen by chance given randomization.
p values overestimate baseline differences if extreme values or skewed distribution are present.

answer_text: any differences at baseline must have arisen by chance given randomization
answer_raw: D. any differences at baseline must have arisen by chance given randomization.
explanation_text:
Why No P-Values in an RCT Baseline Table Correct: D. Any baseline differences must have arisen by chance given randomization. In a proper RCT, randomization assigns groups BY CHANCE, so any baseline difference is by definition a chance finding — testing whether chance produced a chance result is meaningless. What matters is whether a difference is large enough to confound, not its p-value.
Why the others are wrong: A. Reporting standard errors doesn’t fix the conceptual problem. B. P-values CAN be calculated for categorical variables (e.g., chi-square). C. Multiple-comparison correction is a real issue elsewhere but isn’t the core reason here. E. The skew/extreme-value claim is a made-up distractor, not the principle.
Hook: randomization already makes baseline differences random — a p-value adds nothing.

stem: A stroke in which of the following arterial territories would result in an inability to read, but with preserved ability to write?
explanation_text:
Alexia Without Agraphia (PCA Stroke) Correct: E. Posterior cerebral artery. A dominant (left) PCA stroke damages the left visual cortex AND the splenium of the corpus callosum. The intact right visual cortex can no longer ship what it sees across the cut splenium to the left-sided language areas — so the patient cannot READ. Writing is spared because language/motor output is untouched: alexia WITHOUT agraphia.
Why the others are wrong: D. MCA strokes hit language cortex directly, causing aphasia (reading AND writing affected). A. Carotid disease usually causes large MCA-type deficits. B. Basilar strokes cause brainstem signs (e.g., locked-in). C. Vertebral strokes cause lateral medullary/cerebellar signs.
Hook: can’t read but can still write = PCA (occipital + splenium disconnection).

explanation_text:
Observational vs RCT: Confounding Correct: D. An unknown variable confounded the non-random results. The cross-sectional and cohort studies were observational, so people who CHOSE the pill likely differed in other ways (healthier lifestyle, higher income) — a confounder faking a benefit. Randomization in the RCT balances those hidden variables and reveals the true (null) effect; the randomized result is the most trustworthy.
Why the others are wrong: A. The company didn’t design or analyze the trial, and bias would more likely push toward a positive result. B. A few subjects guessing assignment is minor and wouldn’t erase a real effect. C. One year matched the positive cohort’s timeframe, so duration isn’t it. E. Regression to the mean doesn’t explain a consistent observational association.
Hook: an observational “benefit” that disappears in an RCT = confounding.

stem: A 26-year-old medical student is struggling with time management and peer-peer interactions on hospital rotations. The student has received feedback that she spends too much time organizing and highlighting her patient care cards and writing and rewriting notes to the exclusion of spending time with patients. She constantly violates duty hours because of a seeming inability to complete her work during the normal day. When given a group presentation assignment, she completed it on her own without telling her peers, "It was just easier to do it myself." Which of the following personality disorders is most consistent with these symptoms?
explanation_text:
Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder (OCPD) Correct: E. OCPD. The pattern: perfectionism that actually impairs task completion (endlessly organizing cards, rewriting notes), preoccupation with order/detail, over-conscientiousness, and inability to delegate (“easier to do it myself”). It is ego-syntonic — she sees her way as correct — and differs from OCD, which has true obsessions and compulsions.
Why the others are wrong: A. Antisocial = disregard for others’ rights, deceit, no remorse. B. Borderline = unstable relationships, affect, identity, impulsivity. C. Paranoid = pervasive distrust/suspiciousness. D. Narcissistic = grandiosity and need for admiration. Her core problem is rigidity/perfectionism.
Hook: perfectionism + can’t delegate + detail obsession (ego-syntonic) = OCPD, not OCD.

stem: A 72-year-old patient developed sudden onset of memory loss, and was unaware of how the patient and spouse arrived at the supermarket. The spouse noted that the patient was able to drive without problem, but appeared anxious during much of the trip. The patient was able to appropriately answer questions, but then didn't remember the conversation. The entire episode lasted three hours, after which time the patient returned to baseline. The most likely diagnosis is:
explanation_text:
Transient Global Amnesia (TGA) Correct: D. Transient global amnesia. Sudden ANTEROGRADE amnesia — the patient keeps asking the same questions and can’t form new memories — yet stays alert, knows who they are, and does complex tasks (driving). It resolves within 24 hours (here 3 hours) with no other neuro deficits. The cause is benign and not fully understood (often after exertion or strong emotion).
Why the others are wrong: A. Presyncope = lightheadedness/near-faint, not isolated amnesia. B. Complicated migraine has aura, headache, and focal signs. C. Complex partial seizure causes impaired awareness/automatisms, is usually shorter with postictal confusion, and recurs. E. Posterior circulation stroke leaves lasting focal deficits, not a clean return to baseline.
Hook: pure short-lived anterograde amnesia, alert, full recovery under 24 h = TGA.

stem: A patient with a history of depression and well-controlled epilepsy underwent numerous antidepressant trials before finally responding to bupropion. Antidepressants not tried included imipramine, nortriptyline, duloxetine, and selegiline. No seizures have occurred during treatment with bupropion SR 100 mg BID. The patient's health insurance provider, however, recommends switching to another antidepressant because of bupropion's well-known tendency to reduce seizure threshold. Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the treating psychiatrist?

options.text: Taper off bupropion SR and monitor
Add a benzodiazepine to raise patient's seizure threshold

explanation_text:
Bupropion & Seizure Risk: Don’t Switch Correct: A. Continue bupropion SR. The patient finally responded after many failed trials, has WELL-CONTROLLED epilepsy, and has had NO seizures on a low, divided dose (100 mg BID of the SR form, which lowers peak levels and seizure risk). Bupropion’s seizure risk is dose-related and low here — clinical judgment, not an insurer’s blanket rule, guides care.
Why the others are wrong: B. Selegiline (an MAOI) adds diet/interaction risk and ditches a working drug. C. Duloxetine throws away a hard-won response for no clear gain. D. Tapering a drug that’s working invites relapse. E. Adding a benzodiazepine risks dependence to “cover” a danger that isn’t actually occurring.
Hook: working treatment + no seizures → continue; don’t switch on theoretical risk.

stem: A 21-year-old patient is brought to the emergency department after having an episode of nausea, sweating and hematemesis. The patient reports recently having severe headaches and numbness in the extremities. Computed tomography scan reveals generalized brain atrophy. Laboratory studies reveal evidence of renal tubular acidosis and a CPK of 3120 meg/L. This presentation is consistent with chronic use of which of the following substances?
explanation_text:
Chronic Inhalant Abuse Correct: E. Inhalants. Chronic inhalant (solvent/“huffing”) abuse ties the findings together: renal tubular acidosis (classically from toluene), diffuse brain atrophy with cognitive change and peripheral numbness, elevated CPK from rhabdomyolysis, plus GI upset/hematemesis. CNS + renal + muscle damage in a young patient points to inhalants.
Why the others are wrong: A. PCP causes nystagmus, agitation, and violence — not RTA or atrophy. B. Amphetamines cause sympathetic overdrive (can raise CPK) but not renal tubular acidosis or diffuse atrophy. D. Cocaine causes ischemia/MI and rhabdo, not RTA. C. Anabolic steroids cause mood/virilization effects, not this organ picture.
Hook: young + renal tubular acidosis + brain atrophy + high CPK = inhalants (toluene).

A patient undergoes a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) and is diagnosed with narcolepsy. What finding on the MSLT would confirm the diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Narcolepsy: MSLT Findings Correct: B. Decreased REM latency. Narcolepsy comes from loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons, letting REM intrude at sleep onset. On the MSLT the hallmark is falling asleep fast AND entering REM abnormally early — ≥2 sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs) with mean sleep latency ≤8 minutes.
Why the others are wrong: A. Sleep latency is DECREASED, not increased (they fall asleep quickly). C. Total REM isn’t reduced — REM just appears too SOON. D. Increased NREM is not the defining feature. E. Sleep efficiency isn’t the diagnostic MSLT criterion.
Hook: narcolepsy = REM comes too fast (short REM latency / SOREMPs).

Which of the following is the most common reason for patients to discontinue selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors early?
explanation_text:
SSRIs: #1 Reason for Early Discontinuation Correct: A. GI distress. Nausea (and loose stools) is the most common early side effect and the top reason patients quit SSRIs in the first weeks — driven by serotonin acting on gut 5-HT3 receptors. It usually FADES over 1–2 weeks, so warn patients, take with food, and start low.
Why the others are wrong: B. Sedation, C. agitation, D. insomnia, and E. jitteriness all occur, but each is a less common cause of early dropout than GI upset. (Sexual side effects tend to drive LATER discontinuation.)
Hook: SSRIs — the gut complains first; nausea is the #1 early dropout reason.

The student wants to conduct a brief cognitive screen. In addition to questions of orientation, which of the following components of the Mini-Mental State Examination would be most helpful in confirming the patient's diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Delirium: Test Attention (Serial 7s) Correct: B. Serial 7s. This patient has delirium (acute, fluctuating, awake all night, misidentifying nurses, pulling lines). The CORE deficit in delirium is INATTENTION, so serial 7s — a sustained-attention task — best confirms it (digit span and months-backward work too).
Why the others are wrong: A. Recall and D. registration test MEMORY, which is the hallmark of dementia, not specific to delirium. C. Metaphors test abstraction and E. sentence completion tests language — neither captures the attentional deficit that defines delirium.
Hook: delirium = a disorder of ATTENTION — probe it with serial 7s.

Which of the following is a pharmacological effect of lithium?
explanation_text:
Lithium’s Molecular Mechanism Correct: E. Glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) inhibition. Two main targets explain lithium’s mood-stabilizing and neuroprotective effects: it INHIBITS GSK-3 and depletes inositol by inhibiting inositol monophosphatase (the “inositol-depletion” hypothesis). GSK-3 inhibition enhances neurotrophic/neuroprotective signaling.
Why the others are wrong: A. PKC inhibition isn’t lithium’s defining action. B. It stabilizes — not breaks down — catenins (GSK-3 inhibition RAISES β-catenin). C. It DECREASES free inositol, not increases it. D. It INHIBITS inositol monophosphatase — the opposite of “activation.”
Hook: lithium = GSK-3 inhibitor + inositol depleter.

Hook: GWAS = hunting common SNPs across the whole genome.

A 32-year-old presents with new-onset headache characterized by unilateral, stabbing eye pain. During these episodes the patient develops runny nose and conjunctival injection on the same side as the headache. These episodes occur every evening after falling asleep and last up to two hours. explanation_text:
Cluster Headache Correct: C. Cluster headache. Classic picture: severe, unilateral, stabbing periorbital pain in short attacks with SAME-side autonomic signs — tearing, conjunctival injection, runny/stuffy nose, ptosis — occurring in clusters, often at the same time each night (can wake from sleep). Treat acute attacks with 100% oxygen and triptans; verapamil prevents.
Why the others are wrong: A. Sleep apnea gives dull morning headaches, not severe unilateral eye pain with autonomic signs. B. Seizures don’t present as stereotyped eye-pain attacks. D. Migraine is longer (4–72 h), throbbing, with nausea/photophobia and a wish to lie still (cluster patients are restless). E. TIAs cause focal deficits, not recurrent headaches.
Hook: unilateral eye pain + tearing/runny nose + nightly clusters = cluster headache.

stem: A patient presents to the psychiatrist with the complaint of, "I think I'm going crazy." The patient reports that she often feels as if she has "no self" and her thoughts are not her own. In fact, she often feels like a robot and as if she is unable to control her body. She states that she knows she has feelings but is not able to feel them, instead feeling emotionally numb, and she frequently feels that her head is "full of cotton." Recently, she has begun having "out of body" experiences. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Depersonalization/Derealization Disorder Correct: E. Depersonalization/derealization disorder. Persistent detachment from one’s own self/body — “no self,” feeling like a robot, emotionally numb, out-of-body experiences (depersonalization) and the world feeling unreal/foggy (derealization), WITH intact reality testing (she knows it’s a feeling, not literally true).
Why the others are wrong: A. Illness anxiety = fear of having a disease. B. Dissociative identity disorder needs two or more distinct identities with amnesia. C. PTSD requires a traumatic event with re-experiencing/avoidance. D. Borderline PD = unstable relationships/affect/identity and impulsivity — absent here.
Hook: feeling like a detached robot but knowing it isn’t real = depersonalization/derealization.

stem: Which of the following neurotransmitters is thought to play a key role in fine-tuning working memory function in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex?
explanation_text:
Dopamine & Working Memory (DLPFC) Correct: B. Dopamine. Dopamine at D1 receptors in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex “fine-tunes” working memory along an inverted-U: too little OR too much impairs it, while an optimal level sustains the persistent neuronal firing that holds information online. DLPFC dopamine dysfunction underlies the cognitive deficits of schizophrenia.
Why the others are wrong: A. Serotonin modulates mood/impulse, not this tuning. C. Nitric oxide is a diffusible gas signal, not the key player. D. Acetylcholine drives attention and declarative memory encoding (Alzheimer’s), not DLPFC working-memory tuning. E. Norepinephrine supports arousal/attention, but dopamine is the DLPFC working-memory player.
Hook: DLPFC working memory runs on a dopamine “inverted-U.”

stem: Which of the following sleep disorders is associated with mild neurocognitive disorder with Lewy bodies?
explanation_text:
REM Sleep Behavior Disorder & Lewy Bodies Correct: E. REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD). The normal muscle paralysis (atonia) of REM sleep is LOST, so patients physically ACT OUT vivid dreams — punching, kicking, shouting. It is strongly tied to synucleinopathies: RBD often PRECEDES Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy by years.
Why the others are wrong: A. Nocturnal seizures are stereotyped/epileptiform, not dream-enactment. B. Nightmare disorder = distressing dreams but WITH preserved atonia (no acting out). C. Restless leg syndrome is an urge to move the legs at rest before sleep. D. Obstructive sleep apnea is airway collapse with snoring/desaturation.
Hook: acting out dreams (lost REM atonia) = RBD — a red flag for Lewy-body/Parkinson disease.

Accepting a small, meaningful hand-knit gift is a minor, usually benign boundary CROSSING. D. A sliding-scale reduced fee is accepted practice, not exploitation. E. Discussing a patient’s sexual feelings IN session is appropriate clinical work (talking about ≠ acting on).

stem: To ensure that a screening test misses only a small number of individuals with an illness, which of the following should be maximized?

Screening Tests: Maximize Sensitivity Correct: A. Sensitivity. A SENSITIVE test rarely misses true cases (few false negatives), so it’s ideal for SCREENING — you want to catch everyone who might have the disease. Memory aid “SnNout”: a Sensitive test, when Negative, rules OUT disease.
Why the others are wrong: B. Specificity minimizes false POSITIVES (good for confirming/ruling IN — “SpPin”), not for avoiding missed cases. C. Reliability is consistency/reproducibility, not case detection. D. Content validity and E. construct validity describe whether a test measures what it intends, not its detection rate.

stem: A researcher is involved in testing a new environmental pollutant found to be a neurotoxin. After injecting the agent into the experimental animal brain, the levels of tyrosine hydroxylase dramatically decrease. Tyrosine Hydroxylase = Catecholamine Marker Correct: A. Dopaminergic. Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) is the RATE-LIMITING enzyme converting tyrosine → L-DOPA, the first step in making dopamine (and then norepinephrine/epinephrine). A toxin that drops TH is hitting catecholamine neurons — dopaminergic neurons are the classic answer (the basis of MPTP-induced parkinsonism).
Why the others are wrong: B. GABAergic neurons use GAD (glutamate → GABA). C. Glutamatergic neurons use glutaminase. D. Histaminergic neurons use histidine decarboxylase. E. Serotonergic neurons use tryptophan hydroxylase — none depend on tyrosine hydroxylase.
Hook: tyrosine hydroxylase = rate-limiting step of the dopamine/catecholamine factory.

stem: A right-handed patient with a history of intractable seizures underwent neurosurgical treatment. In follow-up testing, the blindfolded patient was unable to name objects placed in the left hand, but had no difficulty naming the objects when they were displayed on a screen. What was the site of the surgical intervention?
explanation_text:
Split-Brain: Corpus Callosotomy Correct: B. Corpus callosum. After callosotomy (for intractable seizures) the hemispheres can’t share information. An object in the LEFT hand sends touch info to the RIGHT hemisphere, but LANGUAGE lives in the LEFT hemisphere — with the callosum cut, that info can’t cross, so the patient can’t NAME it. Shown on a screen, the visual route still reaches left-hemisphere language areas, so naming works.
Why the others are wrong: A. Thalamus lesions cause sensory/relay problems, not this disconnection pattern. C. Right parietal lesions cause neglect/spatial deficits. D. Left superior temporal (Wernicke) lesions cause fluent aphasia for ALL input, not a hand-specific deficit. E. Bilateral medial temporal lesions cause amnesia (like H.M.).
Hook: can’t name what’s in the left hand = right hemisphere can’t reach left-hemisphere language (cut corpus callosum).

stem: Which of the following medications is an effective first-line treatment for patients with restless leg syndrome?
explanation_text:
Restless Legs Syndrome: First-Line Correct: B. Pramipexole. RLS — an urge to move the legs at rest, worse in the evening, relieved by movement — responds to dopamine agonists like pramipexole or ropinirole. Always check and replace IRON first (low ferritin worsens RLS).
Why the others are wrong: A. Carbamazepine and D. imipramine aren’t first-line (and TCAs can WORSEN RLS). C. Clonazepam may aid sleep but doesn’t treat the core urge and risks dependence. E. Gabapentin is a legitimate option (especially with painful symptoms), but among these the dopamine agonist pramipexole is the classic first-line answer.
Hook: RLS → dopamine agonist (pramipexole) + fix iron; avoid TCAs.

stem: Degeneration of the dorsal nucleus of thalamus and the mammillary bodies is found in which of the following disorders?
explanation_text:
Wernicke-Korsakoff: Mammillary Bodies Correct: E. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Thiamine (B1) deficiency — classically chronic alcohol use — damages the MAMMILLARY BODIES and the DORSOMEDIAL thalamus. Wernicke (acute) = confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; Korsakoff (chronic) = anterograde amnesia with confabulation. Give thiamine BEFORE glucose.
Why the others are wrong: A. Wilson disease damages the basal ganglia (copper) with movement/psychiatric signs. B. Alzheimer hits the hippocampus/cortex (plaques and tangles). C. Parkinson degenerates the substantia nigra. D. Huntington atrophies the caudate (CAG repeat). None target the mammillary bodies/dorsomedial thalamus.
Hook: mammillary bodies + dorsomedial thalamus + thiamine = Wernicke-Korsakoff.

Compliance therapy improves medication adherence, not the symptoms themselves. C. Cognitive remediation trains neurocognition (attention, memory) for cognitive deficits. D. Supported employment is a vocational/rehab intervention. None specifically target positive symptoms the way CBT does.

stem: Which of the following sleep changes is often seen in depressive disorders?
explanation_text:
Sleep in Depression: Decreased REM Latency Correct: A. Decreased REM latency. In depression, REM sleep begins SOONER after falling asleep (shortened REM latency), with increased REM density and early-morning awakening. Slow-wave (deep) sleep is REDUCED and sleep is fragmented.
Why the others are wrong: B. Total sleep time usually DECREASES (insomnia), not increases — though atypical depression can bring hypersomnia. C. Slow-wave sleep is DECREASED, not increased. D. Nocturnal arousals INCREASE (fragmented sleep), not decrease. E. Core body temperature isn’t the hallmark; the classic finding is the REM shift.
Hook: depression = REM comes early (short REM latency) + less deep sleep.

answer_raw: A. Can the person work effectively with counsel?
explanation_text:
Competency to Stand Trial (Dusky) Correct: A. Can the person work effectively with counsel? Competency to stand trial (the Dusky standard) is about the PRESENT ability to (1) rationally and factually UNDERSTAND the proceedings and (2) ASSIST counsel in one’s own defense. Working with the attorney is exactly this.
Why the others are wrong: B and E. Intent at the time of the crime and understanding the act’s wrongfulness concern CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY / insanity (M’Naghten), not competency. C. Capacity to make TREATMENT decisions is a separate question. D. Waiving Miranda rights at arrest is a different past-state determination. Competency = present, trial-related abilities.
Hook: competency to stand trial = understand the court + help your lawyer NOW (not guilt at the time of the crime).

A 65-year-old patient has fallen several times over the past six months. The patient's mental status exam is normal. Smooth pursuit and saccadic movements are impaired, more prominently for vertical gaze, but full range of motion is easily elicited by doll's head maneuvers. Idiopathic Parkinson = asymmetric resting tremor, good levodopa response, not early falls/vertical gaze palsy. D. Primary progressive aphasia = a language dementia.
Hook: early falls + vertical gaze palsy (overcome by doll’s-head) = PSP.

stem: The psychiatrist is working with a patient who acknowledges that alcohol is causing a problem in life, but reports not being ready to quit drinking. The psychiatrist works diligently to convince the patient to quit drinking. Each week, the patient returns without having made any behavioral change. The patient asks, "Why should | come in for an appointment every week, especially when | am not ready to quit drinking?" The psychiatrist insists that they are making progress. Of note, one of the psychiatrist's parents was an alcoholic and, despite efforts to do so, the psychiatrist was not able to convince the parent to quit drinking before the parent's death. Countertransference Correct: C. Countertransference. Why the others are wrong: A. Resistance is the PATIENT avoiding change, not the therapist’s reaction. B. Transference is the PATIENT projecting feelings about past figures onto the therapist — wrong direction. D. The patient’s internal conflict (ambivalence) is real but isn’t what’s driving the THERAPIST’s behavior.
Hook: therapist’s own feelings leaking onto the patient = countertransference (transference is the patient’s).

Levels of Prevention: Tertiary Correct: C. Tertiary. The disease (diabetes) has ALREADY developed; metformin treats it to limit complications and disability. Treating an established disease to reduce its harm = TERTIARY prevention.
Why the others are wrong: A. Primary prevention stops disease BEFORE it starts (e.g., choosing a weight-neutral antipsychotic, diet/exercise). B. Secondary prevention is early DETECTION in those without symptoms (e.g., screening glucose to catch diabetes early). D. “Quaternary” prevention (avoiding over-medicalization) doesn’t fit — the disease exists and is being treated.
Hook: not sick yet = primary; screen to catch early = secondary; treat existing disease = tertiary.

When asked what precipitates these episodes, they reply, "When we tell him 'no' or he does not get his way." explanation_text:
Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) Correct: D. Oppositional defiant disorder. The “mood swings” are situational — irritable, angry outbursts triggered specifically by limits (being told “no” or not getting his way). That pattern of angry/irritable mood plus argumentative, defiant behavior toward authority is ODD.
Why the others are wrong: A. Bipolar disorder needs sustained, autonomous manic/hypomanic episodes, not tantrums when frustrated. B. Conduct disorder violates others’ basic rights/serious rules (aggression, theft) — more severe. C. Major depression is pervasive low mood, not reactive tantrums. E. ADHD is inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity, not defiance triggered by limits.
Hook: tantrums and defiance triggered by being told “no” = ODD (not bipolar).

A 26-year-old obese patient presents to the emergency department complaining of a severe headache. The patient is otherwise healthy and does not take any medications. Head computed tomography and brain magnetic resonance imaging scans are unrevealing. The only finding on physical examination is shown in the fundoscopic images below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH) Correct: A. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Young, OBESE patient + severe headache + PAPILLEDEMA (swollen optic discs) with NORMAL CT/MRI = IIH (pseudotumor cerebri). CSF opening pressure is high; the danger is vision loss. Treat with weight loss and acetazolamide; avoid tetracyclines and excess vitamin A.
Why the others are wrong: B. Foster Kennedy syndrome = optic ATROPHY in one eye + papilledema in the other from a frontal mass (here imaging is normal, findings bilateral). C. Sagittal sinus thrombosis usually shows on MRV and has clot risk factors. D. Optic neuritis = painful monocular vision loss with an afferent pupillary defect, not bilateral papilledema with normal imaging. E. Diabetic retinopathy shows hemorrhages/exudates, and he’s otherwise healthy.
Hook: obese young patient + headache + papilledema + normal scan = IIH.

stem: An 18-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with a clouded sensorium, agitation and hyperactivity, mild paranoia, pressured speech, and euphoric though labile mood. Physical examination is notable for hypertension, tachycardia, and vertical nystagmus. Which of the following substances was most likely used?
explanation_text:
PCP Intoxication Correct: B. Phencyclidine (PCP). Agitation, paranoia, euphoric-but-labile mood, clouded sensorium, hypertension, tachycardia — and especially VERTICAL nystagmus (PCP can cause vertical, horizontal, or rotary) — plus violence and analgesia point to PCP, an NMDA-receptor antagonist.
Why the others are wrong: A. Flunitrazepam and C. GHB are SEDATIVES (sedation, amnesia, respiratory depression), not this hyperadrenergic/psychotic picture. D. LSD causes vivid visual hallucinations with insight, usually without vertical nystagmus or this autonomic surge. E. MDMA causes euphoria/empathy, hyperthermia, and bruxism, but vertical nystagmus is the PCP tell.
Hook: agitation + vertical nystagmus + analgesia/violence = PCP.

Several of the residents have experienced poor handoffs in which crucial information (active medical issues, new medical changes) was not reported. They predict that handoffs are frequently missed, and that this is a systemic problem on the unit that could be improved. In developing an appropriate Ql project, what should they do next?

Design a protocol to determine the prevalence of missed handoffs on the unit
Theorize potential barriers to handoffs and design an intervention meant to address these
Propose a new handoff process to the other residents and obtain feedback on its acceptability
Approach potential stakeholders to identify "champions" who would help support a new handoff approach

Quality Improvement: Measure First Correct: B. Design a protocol to determine the prevalence of missed handoffs. Hook: in QI (Plan-Do-Study-Act), measure the baseline before you intervene.

Cue-induced craving is classic Pavlovian learning and a major driver of relapse.
Why the others are wrong: A. Operant conditioning is learning from CONSEQUENCES (reward/punishment shaping voluntary behavior), not an automatic cue–response. C. “Drug-seeking behavior” names the action, not the mechanism. D. Contingency management is a TREATMENT that rewards abstinence (operant). E. Desire to socialize doesn’t explain a place-cue triggering craving.

stem: A patient borrowed a friend's light box to attempt bright light therapy for seasonal mood change, and is now complaining of undesirably later sleep onset and later wakening times. Which of the following is the most likely reason for this sleep outcome?

answer_raw: C. Light exposure was too late in the day
explanation_text:
Light Therapy & Circadian Phase Shifting Correct: C. Light exposure was too late in the day. Bright light shifts the circadian clock by TIMING: MORNING light phase-ADVANCES it (earlier sleep/wake), while EVENING light phase-DELAYS it (later sleep onset and later waking) — exactly this patient’s complaint. So the light was used too late.
Why the others are wrong: A/B. Too much or too little lux would change efficacy, not specifically delay the sleep phase. D. Light too EARLY would phase-ADVANCE (earlier sleep), the opposite problem. E. Distance affects intensity but isn’t why the phase delayed.
Hook: morning light = wake earlier; evening light = drift later. For seasonal depression, use light in the MORNING.

He is able to follow commands, and seems to understand the questions. This type of language disorder is consistent with which of the following types of aphasia?

Broca’s (Expressive) Aphasia Correct: B. Broca’s aphasia. Non-fluent, effortful speech — single words/short phrases with word-finding trouble — plus PRESERVED comprehension (follows commands) but IMPAIRED repetition (can’t repeat “no ifs, ands, or buts”). That triad (non-fluent + comprehension intact + repetition impaired) = Broca’s, from a dominant inferior frontal lobe lesion.
Why the others are wrong: C. Wernicke’s is FLUENT but with POOR comprehension (this patient understands). A. Global aphasia impairs both output and comprehension. D. Conduction aphasia is fluent with intact comprehension but a selective repetition deficit. E. Transcortical aphasias SPARE repetition — the opposite of this patient.
Hook: non-fluent + comprehension intact + can’t repeat = Broca’s.

Telling her the feelings “aren’t real” is dismissive and false. D. Coldly pulling back ruptures the alliance without addressing the issue. E. Encouraging the fantasies to deepen the erotic transference is dangerous and unethical.
Hook: therapist attraction → get consultation/supervision (don’t act, abandon, or dismiss).

Although one neuroimaging study was negative, the patient repeatedly requests a new MRI, still concerned there is an undetected tumor. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Illness Anxiety Disorder Correct: B. Illness anxiety disorder. Persistent preoccupation with HAVING a serious disease (a brain tumor) despite minimal or NO somatic symptoms and repeated reassuring negative workups — with care-seeking (demanding repeat MRIs) — is illness anxiety disorder (formerly hypochondriasis). The focus is FEAR of disease, not the symptoms themselves.
Why the others are wrong: A. Delusional disorder is a FIXED, unshakable false belief (this patient still seeks reassurance/testing). C. Somatic symptom disorder centers on distressing actual SYMPTOMS — here there are essentially none. D. GAD is broad worry across many domains, not one feared illness. E. Functional neurological disorder involves real neurologic deficits incompatible with disease.
Hook: fear of disease with no real symptoms + reassurance-seeking = illness anxiety disorder.

Neuropeptide Y is a hypothalamic peptide that STIMULATES appetite (opposite of leptin). E. Cholecystokinin is a GUT hormone giving short-term, meal-related satiety. Only leptin comes from fat and tracks fat stores.
Hook: leptin = fat’s “I’m full, stop eating” signal.

An individual who is afraid of loud noises has a panic attack in a grocery store when a shelving unit crashes to the floor. The individual needs to take a lorazepam immediately, and goes home. Subsequently, the individual avoids the grocery store due to feeling fearful. According to classical conditioning, what is the conditioned stimulus in this scenario?
explanation_text:
Classical Conditioning: The Conditioned Stimulus Correct: D. Grocery store. The loud crash (an unconditioned stimulus) naturally caused panic (unconditioned response). After pairing, the GROCERY STORE — once neutral — now triggers fear/avoidance on its own, making it the CONDITIONED STIMULUS.
Why the others are wrong: B. The loud sound is the UNCONDITIONED stimulus (it caused fear automatically, before any learning). C. The panic attack is the response, not a stimulus. E. The shelving unit is just the source of the loud sound, not the learned cue. A. Lorazepam is the medication taken afterward, outside the conditioning pair.
Hook: the once-neutral cue that now triggers the response = conditioned stimulus (here, the grocery store).

According to Winnicott, if a mother is unable to provide a "holding environment" for her infant, what defensive process is likely to arise in the infant?
explanation_text:
Winnicott: The False Self Correct: A. False self. Winnicott held that “good-enough” mothering provides a HOLDING environment in which the infant’s spontaneous “true self” can develop. When the caregiver fails to provide this, the infant builds a compliant FALSE SELF — adapting to the caregiver’s needs to preserve the bond while masking its authentic self.

Serotonin and E. norepinephrine are modulatory and don’t reproduce the core syndrome. D. Acetylcholine relates to cognition/Alzheimer’s, not the schizophrenia core.
Hook: amphetamine (dopamine) mimics only positive symptoms; PCP/ketamine (NMDA/glutamate) mimics the WHOLE syndrome.

Retrograde amnesia in a patient with Alzheimer disease
Dissociative amnesia in a patient with major depressive disorder
Anterograde amnesia in a patient with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome

answer_raw: C. Dissociative amnesia in a patient with major depressive disorder
explanation_text:
Which Amnesia Is Reversible? Dissociative Correct: C. Dissociative amnesia in a patient with major depressive disorder. Dissociative (psychogenic) amnesia is FUNCTIONAL — memories aren’t destroyed but blocked from access by psychological factors — so it’s the most likely to REVERSE (often as the depression/stressor resolves or with treatment).
Why the others are wrong: A. Anterograde amnesia during anesthesia reflects memories never ENCODED — they can’t be recovered. B. Retrograde amnesia in Alzheimer disease is from progressive, irreversible neurodegeneration. D. Anterograde amnesia in Wernicke-Korsakoff is fixed structural damage (mammillary bodies/thalamus) and largely permanent.
Hook: functional/dissociative amnesia = reversible; structural (Korsakoff, Alzheimer) or never-encoded (anesthesia) = not.

explanation_text:
Malpractice: The Four D’s Correct: C. Breach of duty causing harm. To win a malpractice claim the plaintiff must prove the 4 D’s: a Duty owed (from the doctor–patient relationship), Dereliction of that duty (a breach/deviation from the standard of care), that the breach DIRECTLY caused harm, and resulting Damages. The key is a breach of duty that CAUSES harm.
Why the others are wrong: A. Malicious intent isn’t required — negligence, not intent, is the basis. B. “Physical harm” alone isn’t enough, and harm may be psychological/financial; harm without a caused breach doesn’t qualify. D. Deviation from the standard of care is only ONE element (dereliction) — by itself, without causation and damages, it isn’t sufficient.
Hook: malpractice = the 4 D’s (Duty, Dereliction, Direct causation, Damages).

stem: Which of the following is an example of the "change talk" elicited in motivational interviewing?

options.text: "If I didn't smoke, I could use the money for music."
"l love smoking, nothing you say can make me quit."
"Yes, I know smoking is bad for you, everyone says so."
"All my friends smoke, and I don't want to lose my friends.”

answer_text: "If I didn't smoke, I could use the money for music."
answer_raw: A. "If I didn't smoke, I could use the money for music."
explanation_text:
Motivational Interviewing: Change Talk Correct: A. “If I didn’t smoke, I could use the money for music.” Change talk is the patient’s OWN language favoring change — desire, ability, reasons, or need to change. Imagining a benefit of quitting (money for music) is classic change talk, which the clinician elicits and reinforces.
Why the others are wrong: B. “Nothing you say can make me quit” is sustain talk/resistance — arguing AGAINST change. C. “Yes, everyone says it’s bad” is passive agreement with no personal motivation. D. “I don’t want to lose my friends” is a reason to KEEP smoking (sustain talk). Only A voices the patient’s own motivation to change.
Hook: change talk = the patient arguing FOR change in their own words.

Parental loss due fo an external cause (suicide, homicide or accident) during childhood most elevates the risk for depression as a young adult when the loss occurs at what age?
explanation_text:
Parental Loss & Later Depression Correct: A. Early childhood. Losing a parent to an external cause (suicide, homicide, accident) raises the risk of adult depression MOST when the loss happens in EARLY CHILDHOOD — the youngest children are most developmentally vulnerable, and early disruption of attachment has the longest-lasting impact.
Why the others are wrong: B. Middle childhood, C. early teen, and D. late teen losses are still painful and impactful, but the depression risk is GREATEST for the earliest losses, when coping resources and a stable attachment are least developed.
Hook: the earlier the parental loss, the greater the later depression risk.

stem: Absent gross negligence, dereliction of duty in a malpractice trial is typically established by which of the following?
explanation_text:
Proving Dereliction: Expert Witnesses Correct: B. Testimony of expert witnesses. To establish dereliction of duty (breach of the standard of care), the court relies on EXPERT WITNESS testimony to define what a reasonable practitioner would have done and how the defendant deviated. (Exception: gross negligence so obvious no expert is needed — res ipsa loquitur.)
Why the others are wrong: A. A bad outcome alone doesn’t prove negligence — medicine has bad outcomes without any breach. C. The injured patient’s own testimony can’t establish the professional standard of care. D. Showing alternative practice procedures doesn’t define the standard or prove a breach. Experts set and apply the standard.
Hook: the standard of care (and its breach) is proven by expert witness testimony.
